title: Developer Tools Stack Guide
description: Build a developer tools stack by mapping source control, CI/CD, deployment, data, observability and security requirements. Includes practical integration tests, ownership boundaries and a cost model without unverified market statistics.

sections.title: Version Control Strategy: Git Hosting Options
sections.body: Choose source control around collaboration, access, review requirements and portability. Define branch protections, required checks, CODEOWNERS or equivalent review ownership, secret handling and how external contributors receive access. Pilot the repository workflow with a real change and test how a new engineer can clone, run tests and submit a change. Do not select a platform based on a market-share statistic that is not necessary to the decision.

sections.title: CI/CD Pipeline Design
sections.body: Build a CI pipeline that checks formatting, linting, types, unit tests and security-sensitive changes at the right stage. Make failures explainable and prevent a deploy from proceeding when required checks fail. Test a deliberately failing change, a dependency update and a rollback. Record pipeline duration, flaky-test rate and maintenance ownership before adding more jobs.

sections.title: Code Quality & Review Automation
sections.body: Automated quality checks should match the languages and risks in the repository. Establish baseline rules, decide which findings block a merge and define how exceptions expire. Test whether the checks produce actionable results rather than noisy warnings. Assign owners for dependency updates, vulnerability triage and configuration changes.

sections.title: Deployment & Hosting Architecture
sections.body: Choose hosting and deployment architecture by runtime, network access, background jobs, region, data handling, rollback and operational responsibility. Test preview environments, environment-variable separation, build reproducibility and rollback. Confirm which platform actually serves production and do not treat a repository integration or successful preview as proof that the production domain points to it.

sections.title: Database & Backend Services
sections.body: Select database and backend services by data model, authorization, backup, recovery, migration, region and scaling requirements. Test a representative read/write flow, access denied cases, backup restoration and export. Identify which service owns identity and critical records. Estimate storage, requests, compute and engineering time from a real workload instead of relying on a generic monthly cost claim.

sections.title: Monitoring & Observability Setup
sections.body: Monitoring should cover errors, latency, availability and important business flows. Define what triggers an alert, who receives it and how an incident is acknowledged and resolved. Test a known failure and confirm that the alert contains enough context without exposing secrets or personal data. Review log retention, telemetry costs and the process for removing sensitive fields.

sections.title: Stack Budget: What Developer Tools Cost
sections.body: Calculate total stack cost from the exact services and expected workload: seats, builds, runtime, database, storage, egress, logs, error events, support, backup and security tooling. Include staff time spent maintaining integrations and handling incidents. Use low, expected and peak scenarios; current vendor prices and limits must be checked directly before budget approval.

sections.title: Common Developer Stack Mistakes
sections.body: Common mistakes include selecting tools before mapping the workflow, duplicating systems of record, granting broad service permissions, storing secrets in source control, relying on one administrator and failing to test backups. Avoid integrating every tool on day one. Start with the minimum viable path from a reviewed change to a monitored production release and expand only when a measured need appears.
items: Adopting monorepo tooling before CI/CD supports targeted builds
Choosing a database based on popularity rather than data model fit (relational vs document)
Deploying to production before adding error tracking and monitoring
Paying for all-in-one DevOps platform tiers with unused features
Adopting microservices before achieving product-market fit
Failing to cap CI/CD spending with per-workflow cost tracking

sections.title: Stack Evaluation Scorecard
sections.body: Score candidates on workflow fit, security, reliability, integration effort, data portability, observability and total cost. Define the weights before demos. For each requirement, record the evidence source, test result, limitation, owner and whether it is mandatory. A claim from a product page is a lead to verify, not proof that the deployed configuration meets the requirement.
rows: Engineer-hours to connect with existing stack: API setup, auth, migration
Time from introduction to productive daily use for least experienced engineer
Breaking change frequency per year; upgrade effort per release
How hard to migrate data and workflows? (1-10 where 10 = start from scratch)

sections.title: Startup vs Enterprise Stack Philosophy
sections.body: Small teams often benefit from managed services when they reduce operational burden, while regulated or larger teams may need stronger controls and explicit service commitments. Neither approach is universally best. Document what the team can operate, which failures it can recover from, who owns each component and how the stack can be migrated if a provider no longer fits.

sections.title: Reference architecture acceptance checklist
sections.body: Before launch, verify protected source control, required CI checks, secret storage, separate environments, rollback, database backup and restore, least-privilege access, error alerting, incident ownership, data export and documented vendor terms. Run a failure drill rather than relying on a diagram. Keep an inventory of dependencies, owners, renewal dates and exit steps so the stack remains operable when people or providers change.

author: Marcus Rivera
